To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the more salient of two novel ethnic groups in an illusory correlation experiment is subject to greater cognitive representation, as indicated by less complexity in the corresponding ethnophaulisms.
the greater prototype representation of the more salient ethnic group predicted the illusory correlation and thereby the evaluative responses toward ethnic groups.

(a) the distinctiveness-based illusion effect is predicted by the cognitive representations of ethnic groups, and (b) the more complex cognitive representations are associated with less distinctiveness-based illusions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people think about ethnic groups.
the development of cognitive representations of novel social categories.
the development of stereotypes for novel ethnic minority groups.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the distinctiveness-based illusion of correlation effect is a consequence of the greater prototype representation of the more salient ethnic group.

the present research has demonstrated that the distinctiveness-based illusionary correlation paradigm, as originally proposed by Hamilton and Sherman (1989) can be extended to include cognitive representations as an explanatory variable.
the distinctiveness-based illusionary correlation is a cognitive phenomenon that occurs when a person has a pre-existing cognitive representation of a group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the distinctiveness based illusory correlation task, the more salience the group the less complex the ethnophaulistic terms ascribed to it.
in the absence or lack of any preconceptions, the salience of a group in an illusory correlation task will predict the extent of the prototype representation for that group.
the more salient ethnic group is subject to less complexity in the ascription of ethnophaulisms and greater prototype representation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cognitive representations of ethnic groups can be studied in the absence of prior knowledge about the groups.
the distinctiveness-based illusionary correlation paradigm is a good way to study how cognitive representations are formed and maintained.
the cognitive representations of social group members are more prototypic in the case of smaller groups, which is consistent with the social categorization literature.
